title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary students engineer prompts when using ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a writing task. The core problem is that effective use of generative AI for writing support depends on prompt engineering, yet non-technical student users often have to learn this through trial and error. The study asks what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns appear in their prompt-engineering pathways during a writing task.

The authors conducted a qualitative multiple-case study of four students, analyzing iPad screen recordings and completed writing tasks. Students were asked to write a blog entry using their own words and AI-generated words, but they were not taught how to prompt chatbots beforehand. They used the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly, during a 45-minute after-school classroom session. The analysis focused on the number, type, and sequence of prompts across each student’s interaction pathway with the chatbots.

The participants were four Form One students in a Hong Kong secondary school, described as the highest-achieving students in English within their cohort. The context was a single after-school classroom lesson led by the first author, who was also the students’ teacher. All students were first-time users of these state-of-the-art chatbots for writing, though they had prior experience with other generative AI tools.

The paper concludes that students followed distinct prompt-engineering pathways and generally relied on individual trial-and-error strategies. The authors identified several prompt types, with auto-complete and natural-language-instruction-plus-question prompts being the most common. Some students developed more sophisticated prompting patterns than others, but overall the findings suggest students were not fully exploiting chatbot capabilities. The authors argue that explicit prompt-engineering education is needed in EFL writing classrooms so students can move beyond unsystematic experimentation and use chatbots more effectively to support writing.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI conversational large language model chatbot used for natural-language text generation and dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Secondary school EFL students used ChatGPT for the first time, alongside other chatbots, to help complete a timed blog-writing task while researchers analyzed their prompt engineering pathways.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative case study found that students used ChatGPT as part of a trial-and-error writing process, with some students producing more sophisticated prompt pathways over time by combining auto-complete, natural language instruction, and question formats. The paper did not report comparative writing achievement gains, effect sizes, or statistical tests for ChatGPT specifically; instead it concluded that students need prompt engineering education to use ChatGPT more effectively in EFL writing tasks.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of prompt content, number of prompts, sequencing of prompts, and observed sophistication of prompt engineering during an EFL writing task

identified_tools.name: POE
identified_tools.description: A chatbot platform/app that provides access to a suite of proprietary chatbots through one interface.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used the POE app on iPads to access ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly while completing the same classroom writing task.

findings.finding_summary: The POE-based activity enabled students to interact with multiple chatbots during the writing task, and researchers observed 38 total turns, with 36 coded prompts after excluding 2 accidental clicks. Across POE-mediated use, students showed varied prompt engineering pathways and sometimes switched across chatbots to test outputs, but the paper reported no quantitative learning effect attributable to the platform itself.
findings.measure: Screen-recorded prompt interactions and qualitative pathway analysis during a writing task

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: State-of-the-art generative AI chatbots used for natural-language text generation in writing support.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper also discusses 'other SOTA chatbots' generically and analyzes how first-time student users prompted multiple chatbots to generate ideas and text for EFL blog writing.

findings.finding_summary: Across the four students, researchers coded 36 valid prompt turns and identified six distinct prompt content types plus three more sophisticated combined forms. The study found that students were generally unsophisticated first-time users, relied heavily on auto-complete and auto-complete plus natural language instruction plus question prompts, and learned through trial and error rather than explicit instruction.
findings.measure: Content analysis of prompt types and prompt engineering pathways in EFL writing

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative multiple-case study with n=4 and no causal design, statistical testing, or validated outcome comparisons. It provides useful descriptive evidence about use patterns but not strong effectiveness evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional implications for prompt engineering in EFL writing, but impact on student learning is unclear because no effect sizes or direct achievement gains were reported.
